Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scanning has been found to accurately change the stage or alter the treatment of about one-third of patients with advanced primary rectal cancer. This suggests that PET scanning should be considered part of the standard workup for such patients, particularly if neoadjuvant chemoradiation is being considered as a component of primary management.

In view of this evidence, we recommend incorporating PET scanning into the evaluation process for patients with advanced primary rectal cancer who are considering neoadjuvant chemoradiation. This may involve imaging to assess tumor response and identify patients who would benefit from additional treatment or changes in their treatment plan.

It is essential to note that while PET scanning can provide valuable information about tumor biology, it should not replace other diagnostic methods, such as biopsy and histopathological examination. Patients with advanced primary rectal cancer should be closely monitored for potential responses to neoadjuvant chemoradiation before undergoing PET imaging.

In summary, incorporating PET scanning into the standard workup for patients with advanced primary rectal cancer who are considering neoadjuvant chemoradiation may be a useful strategy to improve our understanding of tumor biology and potentially lead to more effective treatment outcomes.
